theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before any digging for a new underground data cable between two buildings at a school in Linstead, what must be done first?
options: Start digging by hand at the building wall
Find existing services from records and a locator
Order the cable and the ducts from the supplier by phone
Mark the route with paint and dig at once

questions.stem: Why are communication cables usually laid in ducts rather than buried straight in the ground?
options: Ducts make the cable carry its signals much faster
Ducts cost less than the cable itself does
They protect it and let cables be added later
Ducts remove the need for any marker tape

questions.stem: A cable locator swept along the route gives a strong signal across the line of the trench. What should the team do?
options: Dig on quickly with the excavator
Ignore it, as it is probably a pipe
Move the trench a little and carry on
Mark it, then hand dig to expose it

questions.stem: Why is a signal generator often used together with a cable locator?
options: To find lines that give off no signal
To power the locator's screen at night
To test the new cable after it is laid
To warm the ground before digging

questions.stem: A new data duct must run near an existing underground 220 V power cable. Why keep the separation the specification gives?

To cut interference and limit fault harm

So both cables can share one draw pit

questions.stem: The new trench must cross an existing power cable. How should the crossing be made?
options: Lay the duct on top of the power cable
Cut the power cable and rejoin it after
At right angles, with spacing or a barrier
Run the new duct right alongside the power cable

questions.stem: Where should the spoil (the soil dug out) from a cable trench be placed?

Out in the road, for the passing traffic to flatten
Inside the trench at one end

options: Support the sides or cut them back
Wet the sides so the soil holds
Send in the lightest worker only
Work fast and get out by lunch

One cone at each end of the trench only
Nothing, if work stops for lunch

questions.stem: The cable route crosses a public road. What is needed before the road is opened?
options: The road authority's permission
Only the client's spoken agreement
Approval from the cable supplier
A note to the nearest police station

questions.stem: Which kind of duct is most often used for buried communication cables?

Smooth-bore HDPE or PVC duct

Lengths of garden hose

questions.stem: Why are bends in a duct run kept wide and few?

So the trench is easier to dig
So cable pulls in without damage
So the duct can be seen from above

questions.stem: Why is a draw rope left in every duct after it is laid, including the spare ducts?

To show the depth of the duct

questions.stem: After a duct is laid and backfilled, why is a mandrel (test plug) pulled through it?

To clean the outside of the new cable before use
To measure the cable's resistance
To seal both ends of the duct

questions.stem: Why are the ends of the ducts sealed in the draw pits?

To keep out water, silt and rodents
To stop the cable carrying signals
To keep the duct cool in the sun

questions.stem: Why is a layer of fine, stone-free fill placed around the duct before the main backfill?

To lift the duct to the surface
So sharp stones cannot crush it
So a magnet can find the duct

So the duct can move freely later

So the ground does not sink later

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the marker (warning) tape laid in the trench above the duct?
options: To warn a future digger in time
To hold the backfill in place
To carry the signal between pits
To stop roots entering the duct

questions.stem: Which feature should a cable for buried ducts have that an indoor communication cable usually does not?
options: A bright-coloured sheath made for indoor use only
Water blocking and a tough outer sheath
Very thin insulation to save space
A plug already fitted to each end

questions.stem: Why is armoured or rodent-protected cable sometimes chosen for underground runs?
options: It carries more data than plain cable
It is lighter and easier to pull
It resists crushing and gnawing
It needs no duct or draw pits

questions.stem: During a long pull, the winch could easily pull harder than the cable maker allows. What could happen if it does?
options: The pull would take a little longer
The rope would get very dirty and wet
The duct would shift about in the trench
The cable could be stretched or damaged

questions.stem: What does a swivel do, fitted between the pulling rope and the cable grip?
options: Stops twist passing into the cable
Measures the length of cable pulled
Cuts the rope if the cable sticks
Seals the end of the cable

questions.stem: Why is cable-pulling lubricant used on long duct runs?
options: To clean the inside of the duct
To cut friction and pulling force
To make the cable waterproof
To stop the cable being found

options: Pull harder with the vehicle
Cut the cable and rejoin it

Push from the far end with a bar

questions.stem: While pulling from a pit, the crew must keep the cable's bend radius at least 20 times its diameter, as the maker states. For a 15 mm cable, what is the tightest radius allowed?
options: 35 mm
150 mm
20 mm
300 mm

options: It is under tension, which adds stress
The fibres swell while they are moving
Tight bends help it pull faster
The duct shrinks during pulling

questions.stem: Why is a loop of spare cable (slack) left in the draw pits?
options: To make the pit look full
For later joints, repairs or moves
To let water drain from the cable
To earth the cable in the pit

questions.stem: How is the spacing of draw pits decided on a long route?
options: One every metre, whatever the route
Only one at each of the two ends
By the design, from pull length and bends
Wherever the soil along the route happens to be softest

questions.stem: Why are underground cable joints made inside sealed joint closures in pits, not just taped and buried?
options: Tape is too costly to use
Closures make the signal stronger
Buried joints are easy to find
Water must be kept out of the joint

questions.stem: Why is the metal screen or armour of a buried cable bonded to earth where it enters a building, as the design requires?
options: To carry surges, such as from lightning, to earth
To make the cable much easier to pull into the duct
To stop the cable carrying any data
To power the equipment at the far end

questions.stem: Why are surge protectors often fitted where an outside copper communication cable enters a building in Jamaica?
options: To speed up the internet service
Lightning can put surges on long cables
To stop rats and other pests biting through the cable
To boost the signal in wet weather

questions.stem: Why is an all-dielectric fibre cable often chosen for a buried link between two buildings rather than copper data cable?
options: It can be joined by simply twisting the ends
It needs no duct or protection
No surges or interference; longer reach
It can also carry power to the far end

questions.stem: A fibre in the entry box may still be connected to working equipment in the other building. Why must nobody look into its end?
options: The glass may be dusty
The fibre may be cold
It may break the connector

questions.stem: After a buried fibre link is jointed, which instrument shows where along the cable any loss or break is?
options: An OTDR
A clamp meter
A cable locator
A voltage tester

questions.stem: A buried copper multi-pair cable shows low insulation resistance between pairs after a week of heavy rain. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cable has become too long
Water has got in at a joint or damage
The pairs were labelled wrongly
The duct is too large for the cable

questions.stem: Work out the expected loss of a 3 km buried fibre link: fibre at 0.35 dB per km, three splices at 0.1 dB each and two connectors at 0.5 dB each.
A trench is 25 m long, 0.4 m wide and 0.6 m deep. How much soil is dug out?
options: 0.6 m³
2.4 m³
60 m³
6 m³

questions.stem: A duct has an inside area of 1960 mm², and the design lets cables fill 40% of it. What total cable area may be pulled in?
options: 784 mm²
490 mm²
1176 mm²
1960 mm²

questions.stem: Why are buried cables and ducts labelled in every pit and at each end?
options: So the labels show the cable's price
So each can be told apart later
So the pits look neat at handover
So the cable cannot be stolen

questions.stem: Which record helps most when someone must dig near the route in ten years' time?

questions.stem: After a trench across a lawn is backfilled, what should be done before the job is handed over?
options: Leave the spoil heap for the client
Leave the surface low so it settles
Leave the barriers and signs there for good

questions.stem: While digging, a worker uncovers a cable that is not on any record. What is the right action as team leader?
options: Stop, treat it as live, and report it
Cut it to find out whether it is dead

Cover it back over and carry on

questions.stem: A trainee wants to dig with the excavator bucket right up to a located power cable to save time. What do you tell him?
options: Go ahead, if the cable is marked
Stop: hand dig close to the cable

Ask the client to watch him dig

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the route for a buried fibre and copper communication link between two buildings at a hospital in Mandeville, from surveying the site to having the plan approved.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with the client's drawings and the records of existing services from the hospital and the utility companies: power, water, sewer, telephone and any old ducts. I would walk the route with the hospital's facilities staff and scan it with a cable locator and signal generator, marking every service found. I would choose the shortest practical route that avoids roads, tree roots, drains and building foundations, keeps the required separation from power cables and crosses them at right angles. I would decide the duct size and number, including spare ducts, the depth from the specification, the positions of draw pits at the ends, at bends and at the maximum pulling length, and how the cable enters each building. I would check whether any road or public area needs a permit, plan how the hospital's access and emergency routes stay open, and plan the work in phases. Then I would draw the route with the trench, pits, crossings and depths, write a method statement and risk assessment, and send them for approval before any digging.
markingPoints: Gathers service records and scans with locator and signal generator
Chooses a route avoiding obstacles, with separation and right-angle crossings
Decides ducts, spares, depth, pit positions and building entries
Plans permits, access and emergency routes at a hospital
Produces a route drawing, method statement and risk assessment for approval

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of digging and working in trenches and manholes for communication cables, and how each is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Striking buried power cables can cause burns, shock or death, so services are found first, marked, and dug by hand near them, treating any unknown cable as live. Trench sides can collapse and bury a worker, so deeper trenches are shored or cut back, spoil is kept back from the edge, and plant is kept away from the edge. People and vehicles can fall into an open trench, so barriers, signs, lights at night and safe walkways are set up, and trenches are covered when left. Water from heavy rain can flood the trench and weaken the sides, so it is pumped out and the sides checked before re-entry. Manholes are confined spaces where gas can build up or oxygen be short, so the air is tested, ventilation is used, a person stays at the top and a rescue plan is ready. Manual handling of ducts and drums, and the sun and heat, are managed with team lifts, PPE, water and rest. Every worker wears a hard hat, boots, gloves and a high-visibility vest.
markingPoints: Buried power cables: locate, hand dig, treat as live
Collapse: shoring or battering, spoil and plant back from edges
Falls by public and workers: barriers, signs, lights, covers
Flooding: pump out and check sides; manholes: gas test, ventilation, top person, rescue plan
Handling, heat and PPE controls

essays.stem: Explain how existing underground services are found and protected before and during excavation for a new cable route, with particular care for power cables.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work, the team gets drawings and records from the client and the utility companies, while knowing that records are often wrong or out of date. The route is walked to look for clues: covers, meters, poles with cables going down, patched trenches and street lights. Then a trained person sweeps the route with a cable locator, in power mode and radio mode, and uses a signal generator clipped to known cables or pipes or used in induction mode, to trace lines that give no signal of their own. Every service found is marked on the ground with paint or pegs and on the drawing. Near any marked service, digging is done by hand with insulated or suitable hand tools, not with a pick or excavator, to find the exact position and depth. Exposed power cables are treated as live, supported and protected, and never moved or cut. The locator is used again as the trench goes deeper. Any unknown cable stops the work until it is identified and made safe by the owner.
markingPoints: Uses records from the client and utilities, knowing they may be wrong
Walks the route looking for visible clues
Uses a locator and signal generator, and marks services on the ground and drawing
Hand digs near services and treats power cables as live; supports and protects them
Rescans during digging; stops work for unknown cables

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to lay a duct run between two draw pits, from the trench bottom to backfilling, so that cables can be pulled in easily now and later.
essays.modelAnswer: First the trench is dug to the depth and width in the specification, with an even fall where needed, and stones and roots are removed from the bottom. A layer of fine, stone-free bedding such as sand is spread and levelled. The ducts are laid on the bedding in straight lines, with joints made by the maker's method so they are fully pushed home and sealed, and with spacers to keep several ducts apart. Bends are long and gentle, and the number of bends between pits is kept low. The ducts enter the pits cleanly at the right level. A draw rope is pulled through every duct, including spares, and tied off at each end. More bedding is placed over and around the ducts, then the marker tape is laid at the depth given, above the ducts. The rest of the trench is backfilled in layers and compacted. A mandrel is pulled through each duct to prove it is clear and round, the duct ends are sealed, and the run is recorded on the as-built drawing.
markingPoints: Trench to depth, bottom cleared, bedding layer
Ducts straight, jointed properly, spacers, gentle and few bends
Draw rope in every duct, ducts enter pits correctly
Cover bedding, marker tape, layered compacted backfill
Mandrel test, ends sealed, recorded

essays.stem: Explain how to plan and carry out a cable pull through a 150 m duct route with two bends, protecting the cable from damage.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the cable maker's data for the maximum pulling tension and the minimum bend radius while pulling, and check that the duct fill is within the design. I would make sure the ducts were proved clear with a mandrel. The drum would be set up on stands at the end that gives the easiest pull, usually so the bends are near the feeding end, and lined up with the duct so the cable leaves the drum without sharp bends. A pulling grip and swivel would be fitted to the cable end, and a dynamometer or a breakaway link would limit the force. Rollers or a feeding tube would guide the cable into the duct, and lubricant would be applied as it enters. The crew would have one person at the drum, one at each pit along the route and one at the winch, all with radios, so the pull can stop at once. The cable would be pulled steadily without jerks. At the far end, enough slack is left in each pit, the end is sealed, and the cable is checked for damage and labelled.
markingPoints: Uses maker's data for maximum tension and bend radius; checks fill and clear ducts
Sets up drum position and alignment sensibly
Pulling grip, swivel and a way to limit the force
Rollers or guides, lubricant, crew with radios, steady pull
Leaves slack, seals ends, checks and labels the cable

essays.stem: Explain why communication cables must be kept apart from power cables underground, and how the separation and crossings are arranged.
essays.modelAnswer: Power cables carry large currents whose magnetic fields can induce noise into copper communication pairs, spoiling data and voice signals. If a power cable fails, a fault can put dangerous voltage or heat onto a nearby communication cable and harm people working on it far away. Workers digging later to repair one cable could also damage the other if they are packed close together. For these reasons the communication ducts are laid at the separation given by the specification or the utility, usually in their own trench or at a set distance in a shared trench, with power cables normally deeper. Where they must cross, they cross at right angles, not running along each other, with the required gap, and often with a concrete slab, tile or a non-conducting barrier between them. Each system has its own marker tape and its own draw pits, and they are shown clearly on the as-built drawing. Fibre cables without metal parts are less affected, but separation is still kept for safety and for future work.
markingPoints: Induced interference from power cable fields
Danger from power cable faults to people and equipment
Separation as specified, power usually deeper or in its own trench
Crossings at right angles with gap or barrier
Separate tape, pits and clear records; fibre less affected but still separated

essays.stem: Explain the risks that lightning and differences in earth potential pose to buried copper communication cables between buildings, and how the installation is protected. Compare copper with fibre.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica has frequent thunderstorms. A lightning strike near a building, or on the ground near the route, raises the earth around it to a high voltage, while the other building's earth stays lower. A copper cable joining the two buildings connects these different earths, so surge currents and voltages travel along the cable and can destroy switches, phones and alarm panels and give shocks. Even without lightning, small differences between building earths can cause noise and hum on copper links. The installation is protected by bonding the cable's metal screen or armour to the building's main earth where it enters, as the design requires, by fitting surge protection devices on every copper pair at each entry, and by keeping the earth bonding conductors short and straight. Fibre cable with no metal parts (all-dielectric) carries no current at all, so it is not affected by surges or earth differences and needs no surge protection on the link, which is why fibre is usually chosen between buildings.
markingPoints: Lightning raises local earth potential; copper links two different earths
Surges damage equipment and endanger people; noise from earth differences
Bonding screen or armour at entry as designed
Surge protection on copper pairs at each entry, short bonding leads
All-dielectric fibre carries no current, so avoids these risks

essays.stem: Describe the tests carried out on buried communication cables and ducts after installation, and what each test shows.
essays.modelAnswer: Before cable goes in, each duct has a mandrel pulled through it to prove that it is clear, round and not crushed during backfilling. After a copper multi-pair cable is installed and terminated, continuity is checked on every pair to prove there are no breaks, and a wire map shows that pairs are not crossed, reversed or split. Insulation resistance is tested between pairs and to the screen, at a test voltage the cable maker allows, to show that no water has got in and that the sheath was not damaged during pulling; a low reading points to a fault or a wet joint. Loop resistance can be measured and compared with the expected value for the length. For fibre, a light source and power meter measure the total loss of the link, which is compared with a loss budget worked out from the length, joints and connectors. An OTDR trace shows the length, the loss of each splice and connector, and the position of any break or tight bend. All results are recorded on test sheets and handed over.
markingPoints: Mandrel test of ducts
Copper: continuity and wire map
Copper: insulation resistance at a permitted test voltage, shows water or damage
Fibre: light source and power meter against a loss budget
Fibre: OTDR shows length, splice loss, faults; results recorded

essays.stem: Explain what records and labels should be produced when a buried communication cable route is finished, and why they matter to the client and to future workers.
essays.modelAnswer: Every cable is labelled at each end and in every pit with its reference, type and destination, and each duct is labelled with its number, including the spare ducts. Pit covers may be marked to show communication cables. An as-built drawing shows the actual route, measured from fixed points such as building corners, with the depth at intervals, every pit, bend, crossing with other services and road crossing, and the duct numbers and what is in them. Cable records give the cable type, length and drum number, and the slack left in each pit. Test results for every pair or fibre are attached, along with joint and splice records and the photos taken before backfilling. These records matter because a future digger can avoid the cables, a fault can be found quickly from the test results and drawings, new cables can be pulled into the spare ducts without digging, and the client has proof that the work meets the specification. Without them the cables may be cut, and any repair is slow and costly.
markingPoints: Labels on cables at each end and in each pit, and on ducts
As-built drawing with route, offsets, depths, pits, crossings
Cable details, slack, joint records and photos
Test results attached
Explains value: safe digging, fault finding, future use, proof for client

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would organise a crew of five to install 80 m of buried duct and cable across a shopping plaza car park in one day, safely and with little disruption.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the day, I would agree the timing with the plaza management, perhaps starting early or on a quiet day, and get any permits. I would have the route scanned and marked, the materials, plant, barriers and pump on site, and the method statement and risk assessment ready. At the start I would brief the crew on the route, the services found, the hand-dig zones, the traffic plan and each person's role. One person would run traffic and pedestrian control with barriers and signs, two would dig, hand digging near services, one would lay bedding, ducts and draw ropes behind them, and I would check depths, joints and the work as it goes, and keep records. The trench would be opened only in short sections, with each section ducted, backfilled and made safe before the next is opened, so the car park is never blocked and no long trench is left open. In the afternoon the cable would be pulled, tested and labelled. At the end, the surface is reinstated, the site is cleared and the as-built sketch is completed.
markingPoints: Plans timing, permits and materials with the plaza beforehand
Briefs the crew with roles, hazards and the traffic plan
Clear roles: traffic control, digging, laying, checking
Works in short sections, backfilling as it goes, keeping access open
Pulls, tests and labels; reinstates, clears and records

practical1.title: Lay a duct run between two draw pits and pull in a communication cable
practical1.brief: In the Centre's practice yard, the instructor marks a short route (about 10 m) between two draw pits, with a known buried 'service' (a dead cable or pipe laid by the Centre) crossing it. The trench is kept shallow, within the depth the Centre allows for training, so its sides stay stable. As a team: (1) read the route drawing and write a short risk assessment; (2) sweep the route with a cable locator and signal generator, find and mark the known service; (3) set up barriers and signs; (4) dig the trench, hand digging near the marked service, and keep spoil back from the edge; (5) lay bedding, then the duct with proper joints, a draw rope and a gentle bend into each pit; (6) lay cover bedding and marker tape, and backfill in layers, compacting each one; (7) pull a mandrel through to prove the duct; (8) pull in a short length of communication cable using a pulling grip, swivel and lubricant, keeping within the bend radius, and leave slack in both pits; (9) seal the duct ends, label the cable and sketch the as-built route. Every member takes a turn at locating, digging, laying and pulling. Photograph each stage.
materials: Practice yard route with two draw pits and a known buried service (dead), marked by the instructor
Cable locator and signal generator; marking paint or pegs
Shovels, spade, hand tools, tamper; barriers and signs
Bedding sand, duct lengths with couplers, draw rope, marker tape, duct end seals
Duct mandrel, pulling grip, swivel, cable lubricant, a short length of outdoor communication cable
Cable labels, as-built sketch sheet, tape measure; hard hats, gloves, boots, high-visibility vests; a phone or camera
photos: The route scan, with the located service marked on the ground
The barriered trench, with spoil kept back from the edge
Hand digging near the marked service
Duct laid on bedding with joints, draw rope and the bend into the pit
Marker tape in place and backfill being compacted
The cable being pulled with grip and swivel, and the slack in the pit
Sealed duct ends, labels and the as-built sketch
checklist: Used the locator and signal generator correctly and marked the service
Hand dug near the service and kept spoil back from the edge
Laid bedding and duct correctly, with sound joints and a draw rope
Laid marker tape and backfilled in compacted layers
Proved the duct with a mandrel before pulling
Pulled the cable within its bend radius, using grip, swivel and lubricant
Sealed, labelled and recorded the run on the as-built sketch
safety: Treat every located line as live; hand dig near it and never strike it with a tool
Keep the trench within the depth the Centre allows; keep spoil and people back from the edge
Barriers and signs stay up while the trench is open
Wear hard hats, gloves, safety boots and high-visibility vests; lift duct and drums with care
Nothing in the practice yard is connected to any supply; stop work in heavy rain or lightning

practical2.title: Terminate, test and document a buried copper and fibre link
practical2.brief: The instructor provides a short length of outdoor multi-pair copper cable with a metal screen, and, if the Centre has the equipment, a short outdoor fibre cable, both already pulled between two practice pits and into two training 'building entry' boards. Nothing is connected to any supply or equipment. As a team: (1) prepare each cable end in a sealed joint closure or entry box, keeping its water-blocking intact; (2) bond the cable screen to the board's earth bar at each end, as the training drawing shows; (3) terminate the copper pairs onto the termination blocks in the right order, and fit surge protection modules if the boards have them; (4) test every pair for continuity and wire map, and test insulation resistance between pairs and to the screen with the tester the instructor provides, at the test voltage the cable maker allows; (5) if fibre is used, check the link loss with a light source and power meter and compare it with a loss budget you work out; (6) label the cables, pairs and closures; (7) complete a test record and an as-built drawing of the route with pits, lengths and slack. Each member terminates and tests some pairs, and checks another member's work. Photograph each stage.
materials: Outdoor multi-pair copper cable with metal screen, pulled between two pits and two training entry boards (not connected to anything)
Outdoor fibre cable with pre-terminated ends, light source and power meter (if the Centre has them)
Joint closures or entry boxes, termination blocks, surge protection modules (if fitted), earth bar and bonding leads
Cable strippers, punch-down tool, continuity and wire-map tester, insulation resistance tester
Labels, test record sheets and drawing sheets
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The prepared cable end in the closure, with water-blocking intact
The screen bonded to the earth bar
The pairs terminated on the block in order
The continuity or wire-map test in progress
The insulation resistance test, with the reading visible
The completed labels, test record and as-built drawing
checklist: Prepared the cable end neatly without damaging cores or water-blocking
Bonded the screen correctly to the earth bar

Carried out the insulation resistance test safely, at the allowed test voltage, with no one touching the cable

safety: The cables are not connected to any supply or equipment
